claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles have an overall homogeneous elemental distribution.
Nanoscale compositional fluctuations are inevitable within these Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Nanoscale compositional fluctuations produce spatial variations in metal–metal cohesive energy.
The constituent metals have meaningfully different cohesive energies.
Cu is the lower-cohesive-energy constituent relevant to premelting in this alloy.
Minor local Cu enrichment weakens bonding relative to the surrounding Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu material.
Cu-enriched regions begin to melt before the rest of the nanoparticle and below its global melting point.
Defects created by localized premelting initiate a cascade that drives the overall phase transition.
Localized Cu-associated premelting governs the overall thermal response of the nanoparticles.
Controlled cooling can consolidate a single-phase high-entropy-alloy solid solution.
Using an inert atmosphere ensures that the measured thermal effects are intrinsic rather than caused by oxidation or contamination.
In situ heating measurements will show localized melting initiation correlated with relatively high local Cu concentration.
The Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will exhibit a staggered melting profile.
Premelting in weakly bonded regions will be detectable at a lower temperature than the baseline transition.
The selected single-metal or binary-alloy baseline has a uniform melting transition without pronounced localized premelting.
Heterogeneous premelting in the HEA contrasts with more uniform melting in single-metal nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism is significant for Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm because compositional fluctuations are not fully averaged out at that scale.
The mechanism may cease to apply at larger particle sizes or in alloys with less disparity in elemental cohesive energies.
